title: Candidate vignette and uncertainties (runtime lead loop)
body:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad after the loop with the runtime lead candidate. This is my messy brain dump — for the panel, hiring manager, and for deciding whether to invite for a second round (design + take-home).

Short vignette (how the candidate showed up):
- Candidate framed prior work as: shipping a low-latency transformer inference service for an internal product at a payments company (2 small GPU clusters).
- Comfortable talking about throughput SLOs and how they instrumented tail latency (p95/p99) using heat maps.
- Less confident on edge cases: specifically cache invalidation for KV cache on model hot-reloads.

What I liked (strength notes):
- Clear ownership stories: named specific metrics (p99 target, cost-per-token reduction) and described tradeoffs when batching vs. single-request optimizations.
- Hands-on familiarity with pipeline telemetry: explained a lightweight p99 tracer and how they used mutex-free metrics to avoid overhead.
- Pragmatic about rollouts: suggested an automated canary that compares token-level perplexity on a holdout prompt set before switching routing.

Unresolved / concerns (red flags):
- Quantization knowledge seemed high-level: candidate talked about 8-bit quantization in abstract but couldn't name a concrete library or a recent quantization bug they had fixed.
- KV cache invalidation: their approach assumed exclusive control of model process lifecycle; didn't account for multi-tenant warm caches or rolling restarts where LRU eviction interacts with request-level routing.
- Limited distributed-systems debugging examples: only one example, and it was a single-region outage with easy root cause (OOM). Not much on complex cascading failures or circuit-breaker strategy under noisy neighbors.

Scoring sketch (1-5, rough):
- System design / architecture: 4 (good instincts, clear diagrams in whiteboard, misses in multi-tenant cache nuance)
- Production readiness / ops: 4 (telemetry + rollout thinking solid, limited experience with large-scale incidents)
- ML inference knowledge: 3 (understands costs, batching, but shallow on quantization / kernel-level tradeoffs)
- Communication / collaboration: 5 (concise, took feedback well, pragmatic)

Sample quotes to capture tone:
- "We used prefix caching aggressively — it cut p95 by about 30% for our synchronous path."
- "If a quantization bug shows up, we roll back to the full model and run regression tests against a curated prompt set."

Take-home assignment proposal (my draft):
- Short: Implement a tiny inference shim (Python + mock model) exposing a KV cache component and demonstrate two scenarios: (1) rolling restart with warm caches preserved vs. (2) eviction when node capacity drops. Include a small writeup on correctness and a perf table. Timebox: 4 hours to implement + 1 hour writeup.
- Why: forces them to demonstrate cache reasoning and simple engineering hygiene (tests, instrumentation), without requiring heavy quantization tooling.

Action items (who-does-what):
- Me (Daphne): share this note with Marcus + Ariane and ask HM whether we want a second-round deep-dive on quantization or an ops-focused take-home. (Due: 2026-03-12)
- Marcus: if HM agrees, run a short 30-minute sync to align acceptance criteria for the take-home.
- Candidate follow-up: ask candidate to provide a short list of libraries/tools they used for quantization and one post-mortem (if available).

Notes to self / heuristics I used while grading: 
- Favor candidates who can point to a concrete incident they debugged (not hypotheticals).
- Give weight to small reproducible artifacts (scripts, tests) over long-winded designs without implementation history.

Open questions to resolve before moving forward:
- Does the hiring manager want stronger kernel/quantization signals (i.e., require explicit lib/patch experience) or is ops/runbook experience sufficient?
- How strict should take-home timebox be? we want signal but don't want to bias against people with caring responsibilities.

Raw timeline snippets (timestamps from interview):
- 00:06 – Candidate starts with a clear narrative: "we had to get p99 under 500ms" and shows the metrics dashboard idea.
- 00:28 – Whiteboard: batching + async task queue; wrote a simple state machine for request routing to GPU pool.
- 00:41 – Question on cache invalidation; candidate proposes eviction by lease but couldn't detail cross-node lease renewal.

Final gut call: go to a targeted second round focused on one of two tracks — (A) a 60–90m quantization + kernel tradeoffs discussion with a senior inference engineer; or (B) an ops-heavy take-home centered on cache correctness and rollout strategies. Leaning toward (B) given immediate needs on the team, but confirm with HM.

End of scratchpad. Leave loose; will prune and formalize if HM wants to proceed.

---
Context links: posted the short summary into #hiring-runtime as an async note, pinged Marcus for recruiter next steps.
summary: Informal post-loop notes for runtime lead candidate. Strengths in telemetry and rollout; gaps in quantization and distributed cache invalidation. Recommend targeted second round (ops take-home preferred).
